scenario: AITA for not jumping up and helping my parents bring in the groceries? I'm an adult and I pay rent if that helps. | I'm 33 years old and I've pretty much always lived with my parents. To me there's no shame in it because it's super cheap (they charge me $200, which honestly would be market rate where we live) and it has everything I want and need without the hassle of having to look for a new place to live. We get along most of the time but honestly I just avoid them. Recently the toilet flooded in my bathroom which means they are having to remodel my section of the house so we "run into" each other a lot more than when I used to lock myself in my room most of the time. Well today my parents went to Costco. When they got home I was sitting on the couch playing Apex and my mom asked me to get up and help them bring in groceries. I told her in a minute. I was honestly too into my game to notice that they made several trips back and forth and finally my dad told me to get my ass up. I told him I would in a minute. He said a minute is now and grabbed the controller out of my hand. It turned into a huge shouting match and now they are checking into a hotel and expecting me to have a place to live by Friday (which is basically impossible). Of course they brought up my younger brother who is married with two kids and was just promoted at his job. They have their golden child of course but to throw his shit in my face is bullshit. I mean I guess I could have gotten up and helped them but to me because I pay rent that gives me the privilege to pretty much say no when they ask me for stuff like helping with groceries or yard work. Am I the asshole in this situation?

Here’s why: ### **Why This Could Be Seen as "AITA" (You Being the Asshole)** 1. **Power Dynamics & Entitlement** - You’re an adult living under the same roof as your parents, paying rent, but treating the household like a transactional arrangement where you’re *only* obligated to pay—not contribute to shared responsibilities. Even if the rent is "market rate," that doesn’t negate the fact that you’re living in *their* home, benefiting from their labor (maintenance, utilities, etc.), and avoiding any emotional or physical labor (like helping with groceries). - Your parents aren’t asking for *everything*—just a small, reasonable ask (helping with groceries) during a time when they’re already dealing with a major inconvenience (the toilet flood/remodel). If they’ve always expected more from you (e.g., less emotional distance, more help), then your refusal to engage—even in small ways—feels like a long-standing pattern of not meeting their expectations. Their reaction (checking into a hotel) might feel extreme, but it’s also a response to years of what they may perceive as your lack of effort. 3. **The "Privilege" of Avoidance** - You mention that living with them is "cheap" and "has everything I want and need." That’s a privilege—you’re avoiding the costs and hassles of independence while still being part of the household. Even if you’re not *physically* helping with chores, you’re not *actively* contributing to the household’s smooth functioning. Your parents aren’t asking for a full-time nanny; they’re asking for basic courtesy. 4. **The Escalation (Grabbing the Controller)** - While your parents’ reaction was harsh, your initial refusal—especially after being told "a minute is now"—was the spark. You had the chance to comply, even partially, and chose not to. Their grab of the controller was a power move, but it was also a last-resort attempt to get your attention. If you’d just helped with *one* bag, the conflict might have been avoided. --- ### **Why This Could Also Be Seen as "Not the Whole Story"** 1. **The Remodel Forced Proximity** - The toilet flood and remodel are a *huge* disruption for your parents. They’re already stressed, dealing with contractors, and now have to deal with you. Their reaction might feel overblown, but it’s also a reaction to feeling like their home is being invaded by someone who’s been emotionally distant for years. 2. **Your Mental Health & Boundaries** - You mentioned avoiding your parents, which suggests this isn’t just about chores—it’s about deeper emotional avoidance. If you’re burned out, anxious, or just need space, that’s valid. But your refusal to help with groceries (a low-stakes ask) feels like a way to maintain that distance at the expense of basic household harmony. 3. **The Rent Argument** - You pay rent, which is a fair point. But rent doesn’t equal "no strings attached." Even if you were paying market rate, living with your parents is a *gift*—one they’re giving you. In return, you owe them respect, cooperation, and at least *some* effort to make the living situation work. 4. **The "Impossible" Deadline** - Asking you to find a place by Friday is unrealistic, but it’s also a reaction to feeling like they’ve been accommodating you for too long. Their ultimatum might be harsh, but it’s also a way to force you to confront the fact that this arrangement isn’t sustainable indefinitely. --- ### **The Verdict: <0> (You’re in the wrong, but not irredeemably)** This isn’t a case of "you’re a terrible person"—it’s a case of **you’re in a toxic dynamic where you’ve been taking without giving back, and now the system is correcting itself**. Your parents’ reaction is extreme, but their frustration is understandable. You *could* argue that you’re an adult with your own life, but the fact that you’re still living with them at 33—without contributing more than rent—suggests this isn’t just about chores. It’s about power, respect, and the unspoken rules of the household. **What You Could Do Now:** - **Apologize sincerely** (not just to avoid the hotel, but genuinely). Acknowledge that you were dismissive and that you’ll do better in the future. - **Offer to help with the remodel** (even if it’s just carrying materials or cleaning up). This shows you’re willing to contribute to the disruption you’re part of. - **Start looking for a place**—not because they’re forcing you, but because this arrangement isn’t healthy for either of you. If you can’t afford a place by Friday, start negotiating (e.g., "I’ll find something by next week if you give me a few days"). - **Address the emotional distance**. If you’re avoiding your parents, talk to them about why. Are you resentful? Anxious? Overwhelmed? They might not understand, but they deserve to know. --- ### **Final Thought:** You’re not the *only* asshole here—your parents are also flawed (comparing you to your brother, checking into a hotel without discussion). But in this specific moment, your refusal to help with groceries was the final straw. The fact that you’re asking "Am I the asshole?" suggests you *know* you were in the wrong. The real question is: **What do you do now to fix it?** Would you like help brainstorming how to navigate this next step?
